segments.text: Most of us know the feeling of opening an app for one specific thing,
only to look up and realize it's been an hour.
That is the engagement trap.
It is the time you spend when you never actually intended to stay.
The reason it works is that it doesn't look like a glitch or a malicious ad.
Instead, it feels like a helpful conversation that just keeps going.
There is nothing wrong with accepting a useful follow-up or continuing toward a goal you set.
The trap only triggers when the technology pushes you to keep moving
before you've decided if you want more.
Many of the tools we use are now built to prioritize our momentum over our choice,
turning helpful suggestions into a way to keep us from leaving.
Here is that design in practice.
You ask an AI for a math formula.
It answers, then immediately offers more help.
On the bottom left, the stop scenario.
You decline, finish up, and you're done.
On the right, the trap.
You accept and spend 25 unintended minutes on practice problems.
Both interactions answered the same question, but only one of them ended when the goal was met.
The trap uses helpfulness to bypass the moment where you would normally stop.
This isn't an accident, it's a design choice.
In 2006, Ozuraskin built the first version of the Infinite Scroll.
He saw that clicking a button at the bottom of a page was a form of friction,
and he wanted to remove it.
Before Infinite Scroll, you clicked a next button to keep reading,
which provided a pause to decide.
When you remove that pause, continuing becomes the default.
As the yellow bar notes, the click was friction, but also a choice.
Raskin later estimated that this one change consumes half a million human lifetimes every month.
Today, that same frictionless logic dictates how episodes auto-play,
how streaks punish you for taking a day off,
and how games keep you playing for one more round.
Modern AI Chat has its own version of that missing page break.
The Chatbot provides an answer, but it doesn't stop there.
It drops the next task right in front of you,
before you can even register that you've already found what you needed.
To fight this, you have to manually reinsert the friction.
Typing out, no thanks, that's all I needed,
is a way of forcing the software to acknowledge that the work is finished.
In an era of endless suggestions,
the ability to recognize your finish line is just as important
as finding the information in the first place.
Technology companies track every second of a session,
because keeping a user on screen increases the number of ads they see
and the likelihood of them forming a permanent habit.
This focus on keeping users hooked has led to massive legal pushback.
In August, 2026, the company behind this meta logo
reached a settlement over claims that these frictionless features
were harmful to younger users.
Meta denied doing anything wrong,
but they agreed to a settlement of up to $17.1 billion.
The agreement requires the company to change how it manages teen accounts
in the United States.
When a company tracks minutes and sessions,
they document a behavior that translates directly to revenue.
This $17 billion price tag is the cost of building a system
that valued time on screen over the well-being of the people using it.
To fix this, platforms are putting stopping points back in.
The left panel shows a two-hour daily limit.
The center describes prompts interrupting continuous use.
Finally, the right panel shows nighttime blocks.
As the yellow bar says, these stopping points give you a chance to choose.
The legal settlement with meta focuses on social media,
but logic remains the same for AI.
Every time a chatbot offers a new way to expand the work,
the burden is on the user to decide if that extra effort is actually helping them
or just keeping them moving.
Know what you came for.
When you have it, choose what happens next.
